design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA cited as a guide; no protocol or registration stated) of cardiovascular and respiratory effects of cannabis by route of administration in articles from 2009 to 2023: 42 sources (6 case reports or case series, 21 literature reviews and 15 empirical studies), summarised in three tables and narrative text, with no pooled estimates and no risk-of-bias appraisal of the included studies reported.
can_establish: Which studies, among those its search found, reported heart or breathing effects of cannabis by route (smoking, vaping, eating, dabbing), and what each reported, as the review relays it.
cannot_establish: Whether heart or breathing risks differ between routes, or how large any risk is: routes were compared within one study only in a small laboratory crossover and a perceived-harm survey, most sources are cross-sectional, retrospective, case reports or other reviews, nothing was pooled or appraised, the search string excluded the term tobacco, some included cases involved synthetic cannabinoids or other drugs, and most oral-route data concern young children.

sample.recruitment: Database search of Web of Science, ProQuest, PsycINFO, Embase and Medline (the Methods; the Abstract also names Scopus) in November–December 2019, updated August–December 2023, plus the reference lists of retrieved articles; peer-reviewed English-language articles published January 2009 to December 2023 (p. 1332–1333).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed English articles presenting data on humans exposed to cannabis or cannabis-based products, with cannabis confirmed through drug screening and the route of administration reported. Excluded: opinion pieces, studies including other illicit drugs, and patients with pre-existing cardiovascular or respiratory conditions. Of 110 full texts, 68 were excluded: route not indicated 15, effects not reported 7, other illicit drugs 20, no confirmation of cannabis use 18, published before 2009 8 (Figure 1).
sample.demographics: The primary studies range from children younger than 6 (poison-centre and hospital records) to adults aged 40 or more (Vancouver), college students, Canadian medical cannabis patients and laboratory volunteers; settings in the US, Canada, New Zealand and Italy (Table 4).
sample.selection_effects: In Table 1 the cannabis search terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco, which would drop records that mention tobacco, the main co-exposure of smoked cannabis; the Embase string required both cardiovascular and respiratory terms; English only, from 2009. Several studies within the window and topic, read for this library, are not among the 42 (editors' observation): Monte 2019 (emergency visits after eating against inhaling cannabis), Braymiller 2020 (vaping cannabis and bronchitic symptoms), Spindle 2018 (smoked against vaporised cannabis in the laboratory) and Ghasemiesfe 2018 (systematic review of respiratory outcomes). The criteria were applied unevenly: included case reports involve synthetic cannabinoids, LSD and mushrooms, and most included empirical studies did not confirm cannabis by drug screening. Literature reviews are counted beside the primary studies they summarise, so the same studies appear more than once.

exposure.measurement: As in each source: controlled administration in the two laboratory studies, self-report in surveys and cohorts, poison-centre coding, hospital records and tweets.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Routes as the review groups them: smoking (joints, blunts, pipes), vaping (a vaporizer for dried cannabis in the laboratory study; devices not described elsewhere), oral (edibles, brownies) and dabbing. Amounts, frequency and potency are rarely comparable across sources; doses appear only as study conditions.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco is handled only as each primary study handled it, and the search excluded the term tobacco. Synthetic cannabinoids (spice, K2, AM-2201) appear in included case reports and reviews and are discussed beside cannabis; one included case also took LSD and mushrooms.

comparison.controls: No common comparator: placebo or inactive cannabis (laboratory studies), people who did not use cannabis (cohorts, NHANES, Vancouver), people treated for pneumothorax who did not smoke cannabis, most of whom smoked tobacco (Fiorelli), other routes (Newmeyer; perceived harm in Shiplo), before against after (Van Dam and Earleywine), or none (case reports, poison-centre and hospital series, tweets).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not addressed by the review beyond its exclusion criterion, which was not applied to all included cases.

outcomes.instruments: Whatever each source used: heart rate, blood pressure, chest pain, ECG and troponin in cases; respiratory symptoms, spirometry, expired carbon monoxide, CT and histology, need for respiratory support.
outcomes.operationalization: Any cardiovascular or respiratory effect reported by a source.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; abstract selection was done independently by reviewers (kappa 0.89).

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled. The numbers are those relayed from single studies (see the key findings).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA is cited as a guide.
analysis.selective_reporting: The Methods say the strength of evidence was discussed and graded for each outcome (as insufficient, low, moderate or high, using AHRQ methods), but no grade is reported anywhere in the paper.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The two randomised laboratory studies had 24 and 20 participants (Table 4).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among the 15 empirical studies, routes were compared within the same study only in one laboratory crossover (heart-rate rises similar after smoked, vaporised and oral cannabis against placebo; more expired carbon monoxide after smoking than vaporising; no route effect on breathing rate or blood pressure) and in one perceived-harm survey. The other studies examined one route each, mostly smoking, with cross-sectional, retrospective or case designs. The oral-route breathing data come mostly from records of young children (respiratory depression, need for respiratory support, severe effects at higher doses by body weight).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract concludes that "Cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects" and that edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects (p. 1331). The Discussion says severe cardiovascular effects, including myocardial infarction, arrhythmias and ischemic stroke, were associated with higher THC doses in all routes (p. 1346), and that each route was associated with effects of some kind, "suggesting the need to avoid cannabis use altogether", followed by harm-reduction recommendations (p. 1347). These go beyond the review's own tables: causal wording from designs that, as the authors write, cannot establish temporality (p. 1347); minimal respiratory effects for edibles against its children's data (pp. 1342–1345); and no included empirical study of myocardial infarction or stroke by dose across routes. The recommendations are not derived from a synthesis.

timeline.event: Cooper and Haney: laboratory comparison of cannabis smoked as blunts and as joints (heart rate, expired carbon monoxide, plasma THC); included in this review.
Van Dam and Earleywine: one-month switch to a vaporizer without a control group; included in this review.
Pletcher et al.: CARDIA, 20 years of lung function and cannabis exposure; included in this review.
Newmeyer et al.: double-blind crossover of smoked, vaporised and oral cannabis; Russell et al.: scoping review of routes of administration; both included in this review.
Ghasemiesfe et al.: systematic review and meta-analysis of cannabis use and respiratory outcomes; not among this review's sources.
This review: 42 sources, no pooled estimates; conclusions by route described by its authors as tentative.

replication.where_it_stands: The only review read here that is organised by route. It maps what has been studied rather than measuring risk by route; its route-specific findings rest on a few small or uncontrolled studies and on records of children, and its text misreports several studies against its own tables. Cite it for what single studies report, as relayed, never for a pooled or appraised comparison.

funding.funder: There was no funding for developing this manuscript (as printed).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Illinois Chicago; University of Miami; University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston. No industry ties are declared.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts and controlled studies that measure heart and lung outcomes in the same people across routes (smoked flower, vaped dried cannabis, vaped oil, concentrates, edibles), with use recorded by route, amount and tobacco co-use and a comparison group of people who do not use cannabis, with adults and children analysed separately; and a registered systematic review with risk-of-bias appraisal and a search that does not exclude records mentioning tobacco.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (humans exposed to cannabis), exposure (route) and outcomes (cardiovascular and respiratory effects) are named, but no comparator is defined.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Case reports and reviews were included, with a stated reason, to make the review exhaustive alongside the empirical studies.

Five databases (six in the Abstract) with search strings and reference-list searching, but English only without justification, the cannabis terms combined with AND NOT Tobacco without justification, an Embase string requiring both cardiovascular and respiratory terms, and no grey literature or registries; several relevant studies from the window are missing.
Independent reviewers, discordance resolved by discussion; kappa 0.89 for abstract selection and inclusion.
The independent work described concerns selecting articles; the extraction of study type, route and effects into a matrix is not described as done by two reviewers.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Only counts by reason in the flow diagram; no list of the 68 excluded full texts.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 4 gives design, sample, setting, measures and route for the empirical studies, but comparators, doses and follow-up are uneven; the reviews are described only by purpose and route.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No tool named and no appraisal of any study reported; 'quality indicators' are mentioned without description.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Design limitations are discussed in general, but no study-level risk of bias informs the conclusions; the Abstract states a causal conclusion and the Discussion gives recommendations.
The difference between minimal effects in the empirical studies and major effects in earlier reviews is noted but not investigated; the authors say it leaves the evidence unclear.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (2, protocol; 4, search; 7, excluded studies; 9, risk of bias) and a fifth (13) follows from the missing appraisal, so the confidence is critically low. The review is useful as a map of which route-specific studies exist and what they reported, and its tables are more reliable than its text; it may be cited for single studies as it relays them (second-hand), never for a comparison of risk between routes.

key_findings.finding: Search of five databases (Web of Science, ProQuest, PsycINFO, Embase, Medline; the Abstract also names Scopus) in November–December 2019, updated August–December 2023, plus reference lists; English-language peer-reviewed articles from January 2009 to December 2023. In Table 1 the cannabis terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco; the Embase and Medline strings were adapted to database requirements.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Methods); Methods › Search strategy; Table 1 and its note

key_findings.finding: Inclusion required human data on cannabis or cannabis-based products, cannabis confirmed through drug screening and a reported route; opinion pieces, studies with other illicit drugs and patients with pre-existing cardiovascular or respiratory conditions were excluded. Selection was done independently (kappa 0.89); the strength of evidence was to be graded for each outcome with AHRQ methods, but no grades are reported.

1,873 records (1,811 from databases, 62 from other sources), 990 after duplicates and title screening, 258 abstracts, 110 full texts, 42 included: 6 case reports or case series, 21 literature reviews and 15 empirical studies (2 randomised trials, 5 retrospective analyses, 1 content analysis, 3 longitudinal studies, 3 cross-sectional surveys, 1 pre/post study). Full-text exclusions: route not indicated 15, effects not reported 7, other illicit drugs 20, no confirmation of cannabis use 18, published before 2009 8.
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is an image without a text layer: the counts 1,811, 62, 990, 258 and the five exclusion reasons were read on the rendered page; 1,873, 110 and 42 are also in the text.

key_findings.finding: Smoking was the most common route in the reviews and the empirical studies. The reviews relate smoking to cough, sputum, chronic bronchitis, airway inflammation, dyspnea and COPD, with COPD only with heavy and not occasional or low cumulative use (Joshi 2014); they report vaporizing and edibles as reducing respiratory problems (Russell 2017; Van Dam and Earleywine 2010), and they did not conclusively link cannabis smoking and lung cancer.

Empirical studies by route as listed in the text: smoking (9 studies), vaping (Kaczor 2021, Newmeyer 2017, Pepin 2023, Shiplo 2016), oral (Cao 2016, Kaczor 2021, Newmeyer 2017, Pepin 2023, Shiplo 2016) and dabbing (Cavazos-Rehg 2016). Table 4 gives Kaczor 2021 and Pepin 2023 as edible studies in children and Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 as the vaping study, so the text's vaping list is wrong.
key_findings.locator: Results › Empirical studies, 1st paragraph; Table 4 (Kaczor, Pepin, Van Dam and Earleywine rows)

key_findings.finding: Laboratory comparison of routes (Newmeyer 2017; double-blind, placebo-controlled, double-dummy crossover; 11 adults who smoked cannabis frequently and 9 occasionally): heart rate rose above placebo by 12.2 (smoked) and 10.7 (vaporised) beats a minute at 0.5 h and by 13.0 and 10.2 at 1.5 and 3 h after oral cannabis, not significantly different between routes; no significant effect of route on blood pressure or breathing rate; smoking produced greater increases in expired carbon monoxide than vaporisation from 0.25 to 6 h.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cardiovascular effects, 1st paragraph; Respiratory effects, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 4 (Newmeyer row)

key_findings.finding: Blunts against joints (Cooper and Haney 2009; 24 healthy volunteers; the same cannabis at three strengths including inactive, three puffs): more expired carbon monoxide after blunts at every strength (p ≤ 0.01); joints gave greater increases in plasma THC; heart-rate increases were equivalent for blunts and joints, and the highest strength raised heart rate against inactive cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cardiovascular effects, 2nd paragraph; Respiratory effects, 3rd paragraph; Table 4 (Cooper and Haney row)

key_findings.finding: Smoking and breathing, single studies: NHANES 2007 to 2010 (Kempker 2015): cough, cold, phlegm or respiratory illness in the past 7 days in 16.9%, 22.4%, 26.1% and 24.0% of people who smoked cannabis on 0, 1–5, 6–20 and more than 20 of the past 30 days, wheeze in the past year in 12.4%, 19.8%, 23.3% and 26.5% (as printed, unadjusted); more than 20 joint-years against none, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1 (1.1 to 3.9). Vancouver (Tan 2009; random sample of 878 aged 40 or more): at least 50 cannabis cigarettes and no tobacco, no significantly greater risk of COPD or symptoms; both tobacco and cannabis, COPD OR 2.90 (1.53 to 5.51) and symptoms OR 2.39 (1.58 to 3.62), adjusted for age, asthma and comorbidities.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respiratory effects, 1st paragraph; Table 4 (Kempker and Tan rows)
key_findings.note: The review does not name Tan's comparison group.

key_findings.finding: Smoking and breathing, cohorts and cases: Dunedin (Hancox 2010; 1,037 followed to age 32): cumulative use associated with higher FVC, lung volumes and airway resistance but not with FEV1, the FEV1/FVC ratio or gas transfer. Los Angeles (Tashkin 2012; 299 followed 9.8 years): more chronic bronchitis at follow-up with continued cannabis smoking than in never or former smokers. Naples (Fiorelli 2013; people treated for spontaneous pneumothorax, 13 who smoked cannabis and 140 who did not, 135 of them tobacco smokers): bullae in 8 (62%) against 110 (78%) overall, and under age 35 in 7 of 10 against 3 of 10.

Vaping against smoking, other studies: Shiplo 2016 (online survey of 364 adults approved to use medical cannabis in Canada, April to June 2015): a vaporizer and eating in food were rated lower in perceived harm (cough, phlegm, chest tightness) than smoking, and the number of side effects lower for the vaporizer than for smoking or eating. Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 (pre/post, no control group): 22 people who used cannabis frequently, were not interested in treatment and reported at least two respiratory symptoms used a vaporizer for 1 month; the 12 who did not develop a respiratory illness had fewer symptoms (t(11) = 6.22, p = 0.000065) and higher FVC (t(11) = 2.90, p = 0.007), and FEV1 did not change significantly (t(11) = 1.77, p = 0.053); grams a day fell from 1.75 to 1.46 (t(18) = 1.34, p = 0.10).
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (Shiplo and Van Dam and Earleywine rows)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: two-tailed p for t(11) = 2.90, t(11) = 1.77 and t(18) = 1.34 is about 0.014, 0.10 and 0.20, so three of the printed p values match one-tailed tests; the printed d values equal 2t divided by the square root of the degrees of freedom, a formula for two independent groups (for paired data about 1.8, 0.8 and 0.5); t(18) implies 19 people, while 22 enrolled and 12 are analysed.

key_findings.finding: Oral route, records mostly of young children: Cao 2016 (430 exposures to cannabis food products reported to US poison centres, January 2013 to December 2015): tachycardia in 84, hypertension 7, chest pain 18, chest pain and hypotension 14; respiratory depression in 3, reported only in children aged 5 or younger. Kaczor 2021 (chart review of 32 children): 5 (16%) needed respiratory support. Pepin 2023 (records of 80 children younger than 6 with a known THC dose): tachycardia and hypotension most common; severe cardiovascular toxicity and severe respiratory symptoms (hypoxia, then apnea and bradypnea) at doses above 2 mg/kg.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cardiovascular effects, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 4 (Cao, Kaczor and Pepin rows)
key_findings.note: Cao's printed percentages (tachycardia 31%, hypertension 8%) cannot be reproduced from 430 cases (19.5% and 1.6%; editors' arithmetic). Doses are the children's recorded exposures, reported only as study measures.

key_findings.finding: Dabbing: in a content analysis of tweets (Cavazos-Rehg 2016), coughing was the respiratory effect most often mentioned (807 of 1,179, 68%), followed by lung pain and difficulty breathing; one case report (Rickner 2017; a 17-year-old) describes hypertension, tachycardia, raised troponin and hyperthermia after dabbing.
key_findings.locator: Results › Case reports and case series, 2nd paragraph; Table 2 (Rickner row); Respiratory effects, 4th paragraph; Table 4 (Cavazos-Rehg row)

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: most studies cross-sectional or retrospective, from which temporality cannot be determined; the three longitudinal studies all concerned smoking and breathing; two small randomised trials (n = 24 and, as the Discussion gives it, n = 11); only 5 of the 15 empirical studies reported cardiovascular effects; only three sources specified the type of smoking (joints against blunts); English articles from 2009 to 2023 only.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraphs beginning First, Second and Third; Strength and limitations

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: the Abstract says cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects, that edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects and that conclusions by route remain tentative because of the studies' limitations; the Discussion says severe cardiovascular effects were associated with higher THC doses in all routes, that each route was associated with effects of some kind, suggesting a need to avoid cannabis altogether, and adds harm-reduction recommendations from a clinical reference.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results, Conclusion); Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion, paragraph beginning Nevertheless

key_findings.finding: Funding: there was no funding for developing the manuscript; no potential conflict of interest was reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract lists six databases including Scopus; the Methods list five, without Scopus.
reporting_issues.consequence: The search cannot be reproduced exactly.

reporting_issues.issue: The cannabis search terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco (Table 1) without a stated reason.
reporting_issues.consequence: Records that mention tobacco, which covers much of the literature on smoked cannabis, may have been lost; this may explain why relevant studies from the window are missing.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the strength of evidence was graded for each outcome, but no grade appears in the text or tables.
reporting_issues.consequence: No appraisal of the evidence can be cited from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says no other substance was implicated in any case report, but Table 2 lists a case with synthetic cannabinoids, LSD and mushrooms (Abouchedid 2016), one with several synthetic cannabinoids plus tobacco (Alhadi 2013) and a case series of brownies laced with the synthetic cannabinoid AM-2201 (Obafemi 2015), against the exclusion criterion for other drugs.
reporting_issues.consequence: The case evidence for oral and smoked routes partly concerns synthetic cannabinoids, not cannabis.

reporting_issues.issue: The case series is described as eleven patients, seven men and six women aged 19 to 57 in the text, but as 20–57, five men and six women in Table 2; the text first counts four case reports and one case series, then describes a fifth case report.

The text lists Kaczor 2021 and Pepin 2023 as vaping studies, while Table 4 gives both as edible studies in children; Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 (vaping in Table 4) is missing from the text's vaping list and Tashkin 2012 (smoking in Table 4) from its smoking list.
reporting_issues.consequence: The vaping evidence is three studies (Newmeyer, Shiplo, Van Dam and Earleywine), not the four the text names.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the Newmeyer 2017 sample as n = 11; Table 4 lists 11 frequent and 9 occasional cannabis smokers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the crossover had 20 participants by Table 4 (editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: In the Cao 2016 row, tachycardia 84 is printed as 31% and hypertension 7 as 8% of 430 cases (19.5% and 1.6%; editors' arithmetic), and chest pain appears twice.
The text reports Tan 2009 as smoking cannabis in a joint combined with tobacco, while Table 4 describes people who had smoked both tobacco and cannabis (concurrent use).
reporting_issues.consequence: The finding concerns smoking both, not mixing tobacco into joints.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says Fiorelli 2013 found that cannabis smoking predisposed to bullous lung disease, but Table 4 reports bullae in 62% of people who smoked cannabis against 78% of the comparison group overall, higher only under age 35 (7 of 10 against 3 of 10).
reporting_issues.consequence: The text overstates a small, mixed finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says vaping reduced the grams of cannabis smoked a day (Van Dam and Earleywine 2010); Table 4 shows a marginal, non-significant fall (p = 0.10). The printed statistics mix one- and two-tailed p values and give d values from a formula for independent groups (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The vaporizer findings are weaker than the text says; they come from 12 of 22 people, with no control group.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says only one review (Russell 2017) reported an association between inhaled cannabis and lung cancer, but Table 3 attributes that report to Martinasek 2016 and shows none for Russell 2017.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the lung cancer statements cannot be traced reliably.
